text: In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land, and a man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live for a time in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.

The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the country of Moab and settled there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
The sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years,
and then both Mahlon and Chilion died as well, so the woman was left without her two children and without her husband.
Then she set out with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard there that the LORD had come to the aid of his people and given them food.
So she left the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law with her, and they set out on the road back to the land of Judah.
But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. May the LORD show you kindness, as you have shown to the dead and to me.
May the LORD grant that each of you find rest in the home of a husband." Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud.
They said to her, "No, we will go back with you to your people."
But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why would you come with me? Can I still bear sons who could become your husbands?
Turn back, my daughters. Go. I am too old to have a husband. And even if I thought there was hope for me—even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons—

would you wait for them until they grew up? Would you keep yourselves from marrying for their sake? No, my daughters. It is more bitter for me than for you, for the LORD's hand has gone out against me."
At this they wept aloud again. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.
"Look," said Naomi, "your sister-in-law is going back to her people and her gods. Go back with her."
But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to turn back from following you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me ever so severely if anything but death separates you and me."
When Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more.
So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they arrived in Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred, and the women said, "Can this be Naomi?"

"Do not call me Naomi," she told them. "Call me Mara,* because the Almighty has made my life very bitter.

*Footnote: Naomi means "pleasant"; Mara means "bitter."

versions.text: "Do not call me Naomi," she told them. "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
versions.explanation: The wordplay between the names Naomi ("pleasant") and Mara ("bitter") is central to the verse but is invisible to English hearers. A brief footnote preserves the sense without disturbing the oral flow.

text:
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? The LORD has afflicted me;* the Almighty has brought misfortune upon me."

*Footnote: Or "the LORD has testified against me."

versions.text: I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? The LORD has afflicted me; the Almighty has brought misfortune upon me."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew phrase ‘anah bi carries both the sense of afflicting and of testifying against (a legal image). A footnote noting the alternative preserves the ambiguity of the original.

text: So Naomi returned, and with her was Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, who came back with her from the country of Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem as the barley harvest was beginning.

versions.text: So Naomi returned from the country of Moab, and with her was Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law. They arrived in Bethlehem as the barley harvest was beginning.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew the participle "who returned from the fields of Moab" is attached to Ruth, highlighting her as a returning foreigner; the current rendering shifts it to Naomi alone. Also, "Moabite" is more natural and consistent for contemporary oral reading than the archaic "Moabitess."
